controls.label: Color + brightness
controls.qualification: The star's color, darker where TESS saw it dimmer (contrast drawn stronger) · June and July 2025, mapped in this project
controls.notes: HD 181327 in its own color, darker where its light in TESS's images of June and July 2025 says it was darker. As the star turned once in 1.47 days its light rose and fell by 0.15%. The contrast is drawn far stronger than it is, so the eye can see it: the darkest part gives 0.6% less light than the brightest, and is drawn as a much darker tone of the star's own hue; the Brightness map's scale has the measured values. The longitudes of the darker and brighter parts are measured. Their latitudes and shapes are not: they are the smoothest that reproduce the light. No change of color is drawn, because none is measured. Spots come and go within weeks or months: this is the star then. The darkening toward the edge is the Color dataset's limb law, drawn 1.5 times as strong.

controls.label: Brightness map
controls.qualification: Mapped in this project · TESS mission light curve, sector 13
controls.notes: Where the star's surface was darker and brighter in TESS sector 13, worked out in this project from how its light rose and fell by 0.15% as it turned once in 1.47 days. The light curve is the mission's own; the criteria of Holcomb et al. (2022, ApJ 936, 138) decide that it shows the star turning, and starry finds the map that reproduces it. The longitudes of the dark and bright regions are fixed by the data; their latitudes are not. No tilt of this star's axis is known: the map is made at 60°, the middle tilt of axes that point at random. Step through the 3 maps to see the spots change.
controls.legendNote: Darker: dimmer than the star's mean surface; white: brighter.

controls.label: Color
controls.qualification: Color from Gaia's spectrum of the star; darkening toward the edge from a model atmosphere. The disc itself is unresolved.
controls.notes: The color of Gaia DR3's measured spectrum of the star: a slightly blue-white F-type dwarf. The spin axis is not measured; the display axis is celestial north. The darkening toward the edge is the quadratic law Claret & Bloemen (2011), A&A 529, A75 compute from ATLAS model atmospheres for the Johnson V band at 6,375 K and log g 4.25 (u1 0.363, u2 0.310): a model, because no fit of this star's limb is used.

controls.label: Debris ring · JWST reflectance
controls.notes: The star in its Gaia color, with the ring of debris around it as JWST/NIRCam imaged it behind a coronagraph on 11 October 2023 (programme 2780), in six filters from 1.8 to 4.4 micrometres. It is shown the way Gáspár et al. (2026) show it in their Figure 1: each filter divided by the star's own brightness in it, which leaves how the dust reflects starlight at each wavelength, its albedo, with the filters averaged in pairs into blue, green and red by wavelength. The grains come out nearly white-gray. These are infrared colors, not what an eye would see. Seen from Earth this reproduces their panel. The ring is starlight scattered by dust, about 81 au in radius and tilted 29° from face-on, with a halo of small grains outside it. The images have no third axis, so the depth is inferred: a tilted ring of the measured geometry projects to them better than a spherical shell or the constant depth an extrusion assumes, and each line of sight is placed on it. Which side is nearer to us and how thick the ring is are stated conventions, and the ring is drawn darker than the printed figure so that it stays see-through. Nothing is drawn within 1″ of the star, where the starlight left after subtraction outweighs the dust.
